newsitem.title: CONGO: U.N. starts refugee airlift from Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: U.N. starts refugee airlift from Kabila's Congo.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR began a new operation on Thursday to airlift thousands of Rwandan refugees from the remote northwest of the new Democratic Republic of Congo.
Some 300 Hutu refugees left aboard an Ilyushin-76 plane from Mbandaka, 580 km (360 miles) northeast of the capital Kinshasa on the Zaire river, renamed the Congo by victorious rebels.
They were flown back across Africa's third largest country to Rwanda's capital Kigali. They had fled from Rwanda in 1994.

A few of the weak refugees staggered and almost fell as they climbed the plane's ramp but they all waved as its doors closed at the end of their trek of much more than 1,200 km (740 miles) across the country.
The distance of 1,200 km is as the crow flies from the east of the country near Rwanda's border. But the Hutus took a much longer route through dense jungle and forests.

Almost all the refugees repatriated on the first U.N. flight from Mbandaka on Thursday were young men because women and children died or were lost during the six-month journey since they left camps in the east to escape Tutsi-dominated rebels.

"This is part of our search, rescue and repatriation operation where we are trying to get to the refugees with the help of the local authorities and provide life-saving aid," said UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler.
"They are mostly men because the men are always in better shape. This has been the survival of the fittest," he added.

Mwenze Kongolo, justice commissioner of the victorious Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) led by Laurent Kabila, said many were former Rwandan Hutu soldiers and extremist militiamen who surrendered and were disarmed outside Mbandaka.
The Tutsi-dominated rebels seized the town last week as they closed in on the capital Kinshasa, which fell on Saturday.
"Most of them are men who are strong and we believe this is a group that was armed," Kongolo told reporters.
The French government said earlier this month AFDL troops massacred refugees arriving at Mbandaka.
Kongolo denied this and said the alliance saved the refugees' lives.

"I have talked to the military here and there has been no such thing (as massacres). Our military knows these refugees are men and they are soldiers," said Kongolo, adding he was sent to Mbandaka partly to ascertain the truth of the allegations.
"But we are the ones who discovered the refugees. And we are the ones who told the U.N. So how can you put this together with killing them," he added.

Gabriel Mula Mutya, the newly elected governor of Mbandaka, the capital of Equateur province, told Reuters pockets of the northwest including Bikoro, Irebu and Lukolela were still not in alliance hands.
Mbandaka turned out to welcome the AFDL last week after its former governor left for Kinshasa and Zairean troops retreated on boats down the river following little looting, Mutya said.
The Congo river rolls sluggishly past the centre of town, which appeared sleepy but heavily patrolled by AFDL troops.
On the road to the airport stood a billboard-sized poster of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko in his trademark leopardskin hat. But the picture had been defaced by volleys of bullets.
Some 2,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees were camped near the airport awaiting repatriation on U.N. planes while up to 15,000 were hiding in surrounding forests, according to local authorities.
Refugees started to arrive in Mbandaka six weeks ago. They are collectively accused by many Tutsis of the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda in 1994.
An airlift from the northeastern city of Kisangani slowed down this week when UNHCR emptied the last major refugee site in the area after repatriating more than 34,000 Hutu refugees.
